title: Unipotent orbits on affine schemes are closed
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field]. Let $V$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Assume $V$ is unipotent in the sense of [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure], meaning that all geometric points in a faithful finite-dimensional representation are unipotent matrices. Let $Y$ be an affine scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with a $k$-scheme action $a:V\times_kY\to Y$ satisfying the unit and multiplication identities. For every $y\in Y(k)$, the image of the orbit morphism $V\to Y$, $v\mapsto a(v,y)$, is closed in the underlying topological space of $Y$. With its reduced induced subscheme structure it is a closed subscheme of $Y$ [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction]. No reducedness assumption on $Y$ and no characteristic restriction is imposed.

source.place: Theorem 17.64 (Kostant--Rosenlicht) and its proof, printed pp.373--374; the theorem explicitly allows an affine algebraic scheme, not only an affine variety.

proof.text: Write $O$ for the image of $q:V\to Y$, $v\mapsto vy$. The affine-source separatedness lemma makes $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ separated. The orbit-geometry lemma therefore applies: $O$ is locally closed, $q:V\to O$ is faithfully flat, and its closure and boundary are invariant. Let $X=(\overline O)_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow Y$ and $Z=(\overline O\setminus O)_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow X$. The reduced-induced-closed-subscheme lemma constructs both. Here $O$ is open dense in $X$; in particular $Z$ is a proper closed subset. Both reduced subschemes are invariant, as in the invariant-closure and boundary assertion of the orbit lemma. They inherit actions of $V$. Writing $Y=\operatorname{Spec}B$, the same reduced-subscheme lemma writes $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A=B/J$ reduced. A finite set of algebra generators of $B$ maps to generators of $A$, so $X$ is affine finite type. No reduction of the original $Y$ is assumed.

source.place: Theorem 17.64, pp.373--374, first two sentences; Propositions 7.4--7.5, pp.139--140.

proof.text: Let $I\subset A$ be the radical ideal defining $Z$. It is nonzero: $I=0$ would give $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A=X$, whereas $y\in O$ is outside $Z$. If $Z$ is empty there is already nothing to prove, so suppose otherwise. It suffices to contradict this supposition by finding a nonzero scalar in $I$. The ideal description and the equality $V(I)=Z$ are supplied by the reduced-induced-closed-subscheme lemma.

source.place: Theorem 17.64, p.374, the ideal I(Z) is nonzero.

proof.text: Give $X$ the right action $x\cdot v=v^{-1}x$ and pull it back to $c:A\to A\otimes_k k[V]$. The affine spectrum dictionary and tensor-pushout lemma identify this tensor product with the coordinate ring of $X\times_kV$: maps to any affine scheme are pairs of algebra maps agreeing on $k$. Pulling back the right-action identities gives $(c\otimes1)c=(1\otimes\Delta)c$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)c=1$. Thus the representation/comodule dictionary gives the rational representation $(v f)(x)=f(v^{-1}x)$. Since $Z$ is an invariant closed subscheme, the composite $I\xrightarrow c A\otimes k[V]\to(A/I)\otimes k[V]$ is zero. Its kernel is $I\otimes k[V]$: choose a vector-space complement $A=I\oplus C$, tensor this direct sum, and the quotient map is the identity on the $C$ summand and zero on the $I$ summand. Consequently $I$ is itself a rational submodule. Choose $0\ne h\in I$. Apply the finite-subrepresentation lemma to the singleton $\{h\}$ in this rational module to obtain a nonzero finite-dimensional rational submodule $W\subset I$.

source.place: Chapter 4(d), pp.86--87, coordinate representation of an action; Remark 4.1 and Proposition 4.7/Corollary 4.8; applied in Theorem 17.64, p.374.

proof.text: Choose a basis $W\simeq k^d$, where $d\geq1$. The representation/comodule dictionary turns its rational action into a homomorphism $V\to\operatorname{GL}_{d,k}$. The fixed-vector lemma applies to this representation: $V$ is smooth affine finite type, and the faithful representation in the definition of unipotence is a closed immersion, hence is injective on points over every $k$-algebra; its geometric unipotence includes all $k$-points. We obtain $0\ne f\in W\subset I$ fixed by every $v\in V(k)$. In particular, applying the formula of step 3 to $v^{-1}$ gives $f(vy)=f(y)$ for every $v\in V(k)$.

source.place: Theorem 17.64, p.374, the nonzero fixed function; Proposition 14.3, p.280, and Corollary 14.12, p.283.

proof.text:
The Jacobson-density lemma and the closed-point residue-field lemma show that $V(k)$ is dense in $V$: its closed points are dense and have residue field $k$. By continuity of $q$, $q(V)\subset\overline{q(V(k))}$, so $q(V(k))$ is dense in $X$ since $q(V)=O$ and $O$ is dense. Step 4 says that $f-c$, where $c=f(y)\in k$, vanishes on that dense subset. Its vanishing locus is closed, so it is all of $X$. The radical-ideal description of the reduced induced structure, applied to all of the reduced affine scheme $X$, says that a function vanishing at all its points is zero. Hence $f=c$ in $A$. Since $f

e0$; its inverse in $k$ gives $1=c^{-1}f\in I$, contradicting $Z
e\varnothing$. Thus $Z$ is empty and $O=\overline O$ is closed in $Y$. The reduced-induced-closed-subscheme lemma now gives exactly the claimed closed subscheme structure on this image, including when $Y$ is nonreduced.

source.place: Theorem 17.64, p.374, last three sentences; explicit density argument for the constant function on the reduced orbit closure.

Step 1: affine-source-separated plus smooth-group-orbit-geometry give a locally closed O and an invariant closure/boundary; that node's step 6 shows invariance holds as reduced subschemes. Step 2: I≠0 because y∈O∖Z. Step 3: I checked the right action v^{-1}x, which gives the comodule identities and (vf)(x)=f(v^{-1}x); I⊗k[V] is the kernel over a field; finite-subrepresentation applied to {h} gives W⊂I. Step 4: a closed immersion into GL_n is injective on R-points, so the fixed-vector lemma applies, and its k-point conclusion gives f(vy)=f(y). Step 5: V(k) dense via the Jacobson and residue-field leaves, the nilradical of the reduced A is 0, so f is a nonzero scalar and Z=∅. Edge cases checked: G_a acting on A^2, a nonreduced Y with trivial action, Z empty. No duplicate node found. lean.statement: theorem kostant_rosenlicht_affine_orbits {k : Type u} [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k] (V : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) [IsAffine V.X.left] [Smooth V.X.hom] [ConnectedSpace V.X.left] [LocallyOfFiniteType V.X.hom] [QuasiCompact V.X.hom] (hV : SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent V) (Y : Over (Spec (.of k))) [IsAffine Y.left] [LocallyOfFiniteType Y.hom] [QuasiCompact Y.hom] [ModObj V.X Y] (y : 𝟙_ (Over (Spec (.of k))) ⟶ Y) : IsClosed (Set.range (lift (𝟙 V.X) (toUnit V.X ≫ y) ≫ γ[V.X, Y]).left) ∧ ∃ (O : Scheme.{u}) (j : O ⟶ Y.left), IsReduced O ∧ IsClosedImmersion j ∧ Set.range j = Set.range (lift (𝟙 V.X) (toUnit V.X ≫ y) ≫ γ[V.X, Y]).left
